Subject to any international management / trade controls

documentation.range: Gazella gazella currently occurs in Israel and the Palestinian Territories from the Golan Heights, through Central Israel, the Jordan Valley and northern Negev (Hadas et al. 2015). A few still occur in Jordan, in the Jordan Valley especially near the Jordan and Yarmouk rivers (Amr 2012). In Turkey a small population was reported for the first time in Kirihan district, Hatay province, close to the border with Syria (Kankiliç et al. 2012). There have been no records in Syria since the 1970s (Kingswood et al. 2001), although they may survive on Jabal Hermon and perhaps in upper Galilee (Masseti 2004). In Lebanon, the species was believed to have become extinct after 1945, but three were seen in 1998 in the Barouk Mountains (Kingswood and Khairallah 2001). Gazelles formerly occurred in Sinai (Egypt) but the last records are from 1932 (Saleh 2001). The taxonomic affinity of these gazelles (G. cora or G. gazella) is unconfirmed.
documentation.population:
Numbers in Israel were estimated at 10,000 in the late 1990s (Clark and Frankenberg 2001) but since then they have declined sharply. Annual monitoring transects by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA) counted a total of 1,210 gazelles in the three main populations in March 2015 and estimated a total <3,000 including small and scattered subpopulations (Dr Gila Kahila Bar-Gal, in litt. August 2015). There are no estimates for populations in Turkey or elsewhere but these are considered to be very small (probably <200 in total).

INPA conducts annual monitoring of the three main sub-populations: southern Golan Heights, Ramot Yisaschar (Galilee), Nitzamim coastal plain. Modelling of the Netzamim population shows that it is not growing despite good reproduction, and that if poaching and predation increase it could become extinct within three decades (Dr Gila Kahila Bar-Gal, in litt. August 2015).
documentation.habitats: This gazelle inhabits a range of habitats: hills, mountains, arid plains, and margins of cultivated land. Mountain Gazelles often occur in steep terrain, but avoid rocky areas, and can withstand severe climatic conditions (Mendelssohn et al. 1995).
documentation.threats: The main threats to the species now are illegal hunting, road kills, habitat degradation and fragmentation, factors that are all ongoing. Predation by feral dogs and jackals is a problem in some areas.
documentation.measures: The species is legally protected in all countries but enforcement is not always effective. They occur in small protected areas in Israel: En Gedi (14 km²); Ya’ar Yehudia (62 km²); Mezukai Herev (23 km²).
documentation.use_trade: In Israel the species formerly was hunted under license and was regarded in places as an agricultural pest. Shooting was banned in 1993 due to declining numbers, however poaching for skins, meat, and trophy horns still occurs and is not well regulated at all sites.
documentation.rationale: Mountain Gazelle is listed as Endangered under criterion A2 because the population fell from 10,000 in 2001 to ca 3,000 in 2013, a decline of at least 70% in three generations (15 years). The population is continuing to decline due to poaching, road kills, habitat degradation and fragmentation.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
The taxonomy of genus Gazella is complex and several different arrangements have been proposed, but several issues remain unresolved. Gazella gazella has traditionally included gazelles from Syria and Lebanon southwards through the Arabian Peninsula, with several subspecies named, including G. g. gazella in the north and several others in the south of the distribution range.

Wronski et al. (2010) showed that Gazella gazella consists of two monophyletic lineages: a northern clade (represented by samples from the Golan Heights) and a southern clade (based on samples from the Arabian Peninsula including the southern Arava Valley), based on mtDNA markers. Lerp et al. (2013) produced similar conclusions using nuclear markers and including samples from Central Israel. Analysis of the lectotype of G. arabica (Bärman et al. 2012), a morphological and genetic study of genus Gazella (Bärmann et al. 2013), and a genetic study of gazelles in the southern Levant (Hadas et al. 2015) all further support the existence of two monophyletic lineages: a northern clade (Gazella gazella) and a southern clade (provisionally named G. arabica, from southern Negev through the Arabian Peninsula).

This arrangement is now followed by the IUCN SSC Antelope Specialist Group, with G. gazella replacing G. g. gazella in the former arrangement and G. arabica provisionally retained for the southern clade.
